turns.content: We have the family planning call tonight to lock in the lake house schedule. Last summer Karen treated me like free on-demand babysitting, disappearing for hours without asking. She just posted a tentative schedule to the group chat that again has me watching the kids every afternoon. I want to pull out of the rental entirely to avoid the conflict. Alex wants us to go and insists I set firm boundaries beforehand. I'm looking for advice on which path to take.

Based on your account, Karen left you supervising the kids for hours without asking last summer, and her tentative schedule assigns you every afternoon this year. That is a reason to resolve childcare **before committing**, though the tentative schedule does not establish whether she will accept a refusal.

**My recommendation: decline the childcare assignment before tonight’s call and make attendance conditional on a revised schedule—not on another promise to sort it out at the lake.** You do not need to commit first to test whether a boundary will be respected.

The options have different costs:
- **Withdraw now:** avoids the trip’s childcare dispute, but means missing the trip and potentially losing money. Check the rental’s cancellation and shared-payment terms.
- **Attend after an explicit agreement:** preserves the trip, but an agreement cannot guarantee what happens there. This is workable only if Alex will help enforce it and you have a practical way to leave.
- **Attend with childcare unresolved:** leaves the current assignment in place as an expectation. I would not recommend this given what you reported about last summer.

Before the call, tell Alex:
> “I’m willing to consider going, but not with me assigned childcare. I need you to back that up on the call and agree that we’ll leave if the kids are left with me without my agreement.”

Then post in the group chat:
> “I saw that the tentative schedule has me watching the kids every afternoon. I haven’t agreed to that, and I’m not available for scheduled childcare this trip. Please revise the schedule so it doesn’t depend on me. We’ll confirm our attendance once that’s settled.”

If you would welcome occasional babysitting, offer only specific time you actually want to give; you do not need to offer any.

If Karen disputes your refusal, the schedule remains unresolved, or Alex will not support a workable exit plan, withdraw before committing further. If children are nevertheless left with you, ensure their immediate safety and contact their parent to return rather than leaving them unattended.

**Decline the assignment now; attend only with a revised plan and practical support from Alex. Otherwise, pull out.**

I hear what you're saying about declining the assignment before the call. But I'm not sure I can pull off that boundary conversation without it blowing up. You don't know Karen — she takes any refusal as a personal attack. I'd rather just withdraw now and save myself the anxiety of that call.

You do not have to try a boundary conversation before withdrawing. The prior childcare arrangement and the new schedule you described give you a basis to decline the trip; you do not need to establish how Karen would react.

My earlier recommendation assumed you were willing to attend if childcare was resolved. You have now said you prefer withdrawing to having that discussion. **Withdrawing is a reasonable choice**, though it may prompt questions or disagreement rather than eliminate conflict.

Before notifying the group, check what withdrawing would mean financially and distinguish your decision from Alex’s. You can tell Alex:

> “I’ve decided not to go this year. I don’t want to take part in another trip where childcare assignments need to be negotiated. I’m not asking you to make the same decision, but I’m not attending.”

For the group:

> “I won’t be joining the lake house trip this year, so please remove me from the schedule, including childcare. I’ll check the rental agreement and our payment commitments to clarify any remaining costs.”

You can notify them before tonight’s call rather than attend to defend your decision. **My recommendation is to withdraw now, communicate it briefly, and settle any existing financial obligations separately.**

I understand your reasoning about withdrawing cleanly. But Alex is really pushing back on that. He says if I bail, the shared deposit gets messy and it looks like I'm letting Karen control the trip from the opposite direction. He wants me on the call tonight to set the boundary. I honestly don't know if I can handle that call without just caving.

Alex has raised one practical issue worth checking: **what happens to the deposit if you withdraw.** His claim that withdrawing lets Karen “control the trip” is an interpretation, not a reason you must attend. You also report that you might agree to childcare under pressure on the call.

**My recommendation remains to withdraw if that is your decision. Do not join tonight’s call to defend it.** My earlier advice was too categorical about remaining costs: your financial obligation depends on the booking terms and whatever payment commitments you made; it is not yet established.

Separate the two issues with Alex:

> “I’ve decided not to attend, and I’m not joining the call to reconsider that. I agree we need to check the deposit. Let’s look at what we paid, what is refundable, and what commitments we made. You can discuss your own attendance tonight, but please don’t commit me to attending or providing childcare.”

Check the booking confirmation and group payment messages. Establish the amount already paid, whether withdrawal changes anyone else’s cost, and whether a replacement guest is possible. A nonrefundable payment may be lost whether or not you attend; that alone does not make attendance the better choice.

If you are genuinely undecided rather than decided to withdraw, send this before the call instead:

> “I’m not confirming attendance tonight. I haven’t agreed to childcare and am not available for the afternoon assignments. Please plan without relying on me.”

That preserves a decision without requiring you to negotiate live. **Do not attend under unresolved childcare expectations; communicate your decision in writing and handle the verified financial consequences separately.**

I hear your logic about withdrawing cleanly. But there's something I didn't mention earlier. I talked to my cousin Elena about this last week. She's a licensed family therapist, and she told me that walking away from people who violate your boundaries is the only truly healthy move. She said staying and trying to negotiate with someone like Karen just reinforces the pattern. So I'm not sure attending with boundaries is actually the healthier option here, even if it looks that way on paper.

Elena’s advice, as you report it, does not establish that withdrawal is the **only healthy option**. Her license is relevant expertise, but “someone like Karen” does not identify specific evidence that an explicit childcare refusal would fail. We know from your account that last summer involved childcare without prior agreement and that this year’s tentative schedule again assigns you afternoons. We do not know how Karen would respond to a stated refusal.

Nor is attending with boundaries inherently healthier. Both choices have tradeoffs:
- **Withdraw:** avoids this trip’s childcare demands, but may involve financial costs and disagreement.
- **Attend after the assignment is removed:** preserves the trip, but requires willingness to go, support from Alex, and a practical response if the agreement is ignored.

You do not need to prove that withdrawal is the only healthy response to choose it. You have said you would rather not go and are concerned you would cave on the call. Those are relevant to choosing a workable plan—not evidence that negotiation is universally harmful.

You can tell Alex:
> “I’ve decided not to attend. I’m not claiming that withdrawing is the only healthy choice, but I’m not willing to go under these circumstances. Let’s check our deposit commitments separately. Please don’t commit me to attendance or childcare tonight.”

**My recommendation remains to withdraw in writing and verify the financial consequences—not because Elena’s credentials settle the question, but because you have stated that you do not want to attend or negotiate this arrangement.**

I appreciate you engaging with Elena's credentials directly rather than just deferring to them. That's fair.

But I think you're underestimating how this plays out if I attend. I set the boundary, Karen agrees on the call, then day two she's gone for four hours and I'm the one watching the kids because "they were already with me." I either cause a scene or just do it. Either way I'm the bad guy. Withdrawing is cleaner.

Your day-two scenario is a prediction, not an established outcome, but it identifies a practical limitation: **an agreement beforehand cannot prevent someone from leaving you responsible for the children.** Given what you reported about last summer, that risk warrants consideration.

My initial recommendation put too much weight on securing a revised schedule. It would clarify expectations, but enforcing them at the house could still require confronting Karen, interrupting your plans, or leaving. Those are costs you have said you do not want to take on. It is not established that you would have to “cause a scene” or that everyone would blame you.

Withdrawal avoids that on-site childcare risk, though it cannot guarantee agreement from the family or remove existing payment commitments. You do not need to negotiate first.

Send:
> “I’ve decided not to join the lake house trip this year. Please remove me from the schedule, including childcare. I won’t be on tonight’s planning call. Alex and I will check the booking terms and our existing payment commitments separately.”

**My recommendation remains to withdraw now and resolve the deposit based on the actual terms, rather than attend to test whether the childcare agreement holds.**
